# Use a crab detector

## Background
The aim of this leg of the repository is to go from unseen data to assessment ready data, where unseen video material is the input and the output is the relative abundance indices MaxN and MeanN per BRUV/video station obtained with either the pretrained crab detector, or another model. 

MaxN is the single image frame within a deployment with the highest count of individuals per deployment, wheras MeanN is the mean number of individual observed over a series of image frames [@whitmarsh_what_2017]. MaxN is the most commonly applied metric ofr estimating abundances in video-based surveys, and its conservative with its aim to reduce the likelihood of double counting individuals.

The pretrained crab detector developed in the thesis is included in this repository, in the folder `use-a-crab-detector/model/pretrained-crab-detector`. This model is not yet plug and play, as documented in the thesis, and in the literature more broadly, YOLO models in particular struggle to generalize: when the input material shifts away from the domain it was trained on, performance drops [@lurig_computer_2021]. Specifically, this model was trained to detect brown crab in BRUVs placed in nearshore coastal areas between 62°N and 68°N. When applied outside this scope, whether due to a different video collection method or a different environment, it's going to struggle (see the FjordFish test in Brøten [-@broten_crabs_2026]).

If you'd still like to apply this detector given these caveats, or apply a new (and likely better) model, some manual work is still needed. To interpret the model's predictions, we need some understanding of its generalizability. One important step is building an independent test set: annotate a small subset of unseen data, let the model predict on it, then compare the model's predictions against the human-annotated ground truth.

Recommended running order: 
1. `1-get-ready-to-use-a-crab-detector`
2. `2-use-a-detector`
3. `3-interpret-raw-detections`
4. `4-post-processing-pipeline`


## Before running the detector - independent test set

Often described as the gold standard for evaluating a trained models performance, and applied after a model is fully trained to assess the ability of the model to generalize, and its ability to detect general features rather than memorizing its training data [@biscarini_deep_2026]. In this instance, its purpose is rather to evaluate the models "compatibility" with the data its going to predict upon. The model will predict on a small annotated dataset, and the predictions will be compared to the annotations. All this is done in the script `1-get-ready-to-use-a-crab-detector`.

### Setup an collecting predictions (Chunk 0 -- 3)
To start, you will need a fully annotated dataset and should be around 10 -- 25% of the available data. Alongside this repository is a small dataset which can be applied in the following scripts to test the methods. Likewise to the data processing pipeline performed in `1-raw_to_yolo` the annotations are converted from RLE-masks to bounding boxes, and only the crab annotations are kept. The scrips logic for grouping is still based on the naming convention as previously mentioned, if the dataset uses another naming convention the code needs to be readjusted. The model will then predict on the dataset assigned, these are saved in `use-a-crab-detector/data/test_predictions/predictions.json`.

### Comparing model predictions to human ground truth (Chunk 4 -- 6)

First the per stations maxN, meanN and total crab count from the human-anotated test set is collected, this is the ground truth the predictions are compared against, then the same is done for the models predictions. Duplicated bounding boxes (two bounding boxes overlapping) are removed, and every image at a station is counted even when the model found nothing. As the model predicts it assigns a confidence score to the prediction from 0 -- 1 based on how sure it is, the confidence threshold for predictions can be adjusted. High confidence thresholds keeps only the models most certain predictions (fewer false detections, but real crabs might be missed), wheras low confidence thresholds introduce introduces noise but retains more predictions. Because there is no single correct threshold, the script evaluates several thresholds (none, 0.5 and 0.75 by default) so you can see the trade-off rather than guessing. 

The script saves two things: `threshold_summary.csv`, with one row per threshold
giving the total crab count and average maxN/meanN for both the human annotator alongside three bar charts (`total_crabs_by_station.png`, `maxN_by_station.png`, `meanN_by_station.png`) comparing the human truth against the model at each threshold.

In the thesis, this comparison highlighted that neither a low or a high threshold was able to give an accurate MaxN prediction and highlighting the need for a more flexible solution for interpreting the detentions, this is covered in the post-processing-pipeline. To ruther understand what features drove the detector to make a prediction, a Grad-CAM analysis can be performed, which produces a heatmap highlighting important areas for detection.

## Running the detector 

### Applying the detector to new footage

Once the crab-detector returned acceptable results on the independent testset, `2-use.-crab-detector` runs the model across a full folder of new BRUV videos. Point it (change the path) at the folder containing the desired footage and desired model, its also possible to change the image size, hyperparameters (though these should be close to the initial training setup) and confidence threshold. The script makes the detector predict roughly every second (matching the extraction of training data), but this can be changed, runs the detector on these frames and collects every detection into a single `predictions.json` file. 

The confidence threshold is set to be deliberately low (0.1), hence the script is not deciding what counts as a "real" crab, just recording every prediction. The actual filtering, so choosing a confidence threshold and removing likely false detection happens in the next steps. By default this script only saves the detections and not annotated videos, to activate this there is a toggle in the scripts configuration to save a copy of each video with the predicted videos drawn in, off is the default since it adds significant disk use and processing time.

### Checking what the model found

Before doing any real filtering, it is worth looking at what the detector actually predicted. `3-interpret_detections` reads the `predictions.json` file and reports the total number of detections, how many frames had at least one and how many detections fall above a couple confidence cutoffs (0.5 and 0.75 by default). It plots a histogram of the confidence score of every detection as a sanity check, and should (if you are applying the pretrained model) have a bimodal structure, with a high peak withing the lower end of confidence scores, and a second smaller peak with the higher scores (Figure \@ref(fig:histpreds24)).

```{r histpreds24, echo=FALSE, fig.cap = "Distribution  of confidence scores for crab predictions generated by the object detection model on BRUV videos from the 2024 gill- and fyke-net survey (Brøten, 2026). A confidence score reflects how certain the model is in its prediction of a crab from 0 to 1, where 1 indicates the highest model certainty. Each prediction represents a detection within a single frame, and not necessarily a unique individual."}
knitr::include_graphics("images/confthresholdHistogram.png")

```
In the last chunk it applies a soft tracker to display

Essentially it shows how many consecutive frames a bounding box was present, and with the current crab detector used in the repo there will likely be a big amount of detections appearing for one frame and then disappearing. Since crab are slow movers (or at least slower than moist fish), we can assume that they stay in frame for longer than one second, and three seconds. Hence, all detections that are present for less than three seconds, we can assume were false. Likewise, crabs do move, so detections appearing in the same position for over 500 frames can be assumed to be false - both of these are removed in the post-processing pipeline (Figure \@ref(fig:trackBBox)). 

```{r trackBBox, echo =FALSE, fig.cap=cap, out.width="80%"}
knitr::include_graphics("images/trackBbox.png")

cap <- "Relationship between track length (number of consecutive frames in which a detection appears) and bounding box center dispersion for crab detections generated by the crab detector in Brøten (2026). Dashed lines indicate track length thresholds applied during post-processing of the predictions (3-500 frames)."

```

## Post-processing-pipeline

This step is optional, but shows the workflow for removing likely false detections whilst maximizing the amount of true crab predictions beyoud what confidence thresholding alone could achieve in `4-post-processing-pipeline`

applied in thesis. The idea behind was based on visual observation of the behavior of the crab in the model aswell as the models predictions behavior. To maximize true crab detections beyond what confidence thresholding alone could achieve, a post-processing pipeline was developed based on visual inspection of model predictions and known crab behavior in the BRUV footage.

Occasionally the model produced many overlapping bounding boxes for the same individual crab. This is a common issue with object detection models, and the removal of these are called sequential Non-Maximum Supression, the same technique is applied here and also seen in a study for counting for fish by Connolly et al. [-@connolly_improved_2021].

To address this, deduplication filters were applied within each individual frame with IoU. Pairwise IoU were calculated between all bounding boxes from model inference. Based on comparisons of multiple IoU thresholds, an IoU threshold of 0.3 was found to remove most overlapping bounding boxes, lower than 0.5 used in model evaluation, as the goal was to remove duplicate detections rather than assess accuracy. Only the largest bounding box (by area) was kept under the assumption that it was more likely to contain the entire crab (Figure \@ref(fig:duplicatebbox)). 

```{r duplicatebbox, echo = FALSE,out.width="100%", fig.cap=cap, fig.align='center'}

knitr::include_graphics("images/frame_1_NO_2024_0608_GarnRuse_Edoy_EN5_Ra7_L4_501068451_979.jpg")

cap <- "A random frame from inference on BRUV footage from the 2024 gill- and fyke-net survey, where there are two detections (yellow boxes), and their bounding boxes overlap more than 30% (IoU $\\geq$ 0.3) over the same crab. After applying a post-processing pipeline to remove noise and unlikely predictions of crab, only the largest box of the two is kept."


```

After deduplication, all predictions with a confidence of $\geq$ 0.3 were kept, based on visual inspections that true crab predictions were rarely below this threshold.

The crab's behavior in the BRUV footage differs from fish, they moved slower and stayed in the frame for extended periods. To exploit this behavior, a tracking-based filtering approach was implemented. Detections were linked across consecutive frames into tracks based on the spatial proximity of bounding box centers and bounding box overlap in consecutive frames. Tracks were allowed to persist across short frame gaps (± 2 frames) to account for missed detections. Tracks with a duration of fewer than 3 frames, was assumed to likely represent false detections, and was removed. Conversely, tracks persisting for over 500 frames were also removed as these typically corresponded to static false detections such as substrate features misidentified across the deployment. The predictions that were left after the post-processing pipeline were saved for further analysis. 

The post-processing pipeline therefore consisted of four steps: 1) bounding box deduplication using IoU filtering, 2) confidence thresholding, 3) temporal tracking of detections, and 4) removal of short.

The two last chunks collects a .csv file showing amongst other, the station, raw maxN, filtered maxn, and the frames it appeared. For further analysis doing a e..g  `left_join` with the station for the metadata bout the dattion for furhter analysis.  in rFramewise comparison of the raw maxNs and the filered maxN for visual comparison. The main takeaway form the visual confirmation should be that the filtered predictions generally look better, but there will most likely be errors.
